dashboard.title: Overview
dashboard.intro: A summary of the whole proxy network: how many servers answer, how many keys work, how many people are connected right now and what went wrong. The numbers refresh on their own; the "updated … ago" stamp next to the title says how fresh they are.

nodes_online.name: Reachable servers
nodes_online.what: The number of online servers and the total fleet size. A server that stops responding beyond the offline threshold is marked unavailable. See the server list below for details.
nodes_online.tip: An offline server hands out nothing: clients bound only to it will not connect.

keys_active.name: Active keys
keys_active.what: Keys with Active status. The total number of keys appears below. Open the card to manage keys and inspect pending changes.
keys_active.tip: If the pending count never shrinks, an apply is failing on some server: open the server → Maintenance → Apply history.

people.name: People online
people.what: An estimate of how many people are connected right now. A personal user with at least one connection counts as one person; a shared user counts as many as the distinct IP addresses connected to it. So for a shared user, several people behind one router count as one, while one person's phone on mobile data and computer on Wi-Fi count as two. Someone connected to two servers counts once. tproxy servers count their WEB sessions instead. Updated every minute.
people.tip: The tile's tooltip also shows how many people were online over the last 15 minutes.

connections.name: Connections
connections.what: The line under the head count: TCP connections open right now on all servers that are online. One Telegram app holds several connections at once, usually 2 to 15, so there are always more connections than people.

traffic.name: Traffic, 24 h
traffic.what: Inbound plus outbound traffic of every server over the last 24 hours. Computed from stats snapshots, so it can lag a few minutes.

chart.name: People online over 24 hours
chart.what: How many people were online on each server over the last 24 hours. Each server has its own line; larger fleets group additional servers as Other. Offline servers appear gray. Where the history predates this panel version, the line shows connections. Open Monitoring for detailed charts.

alerts.name: Needs attention
alerts.what: Open notifications about problems. Select a server name to inspect its status. Dismiss notification removes the entry but does not fix the cause.
alerts.tip: The same events arrive in Telegram once notifications are on: Settings → Notifications and polling.

jobs.name: Recent changes
jobs.what: The latest apply jobs on the servers with their result and duration. An "apply" is the moment key and site changes are actually sent to a server.

notes.1: A server that has not been installed yet shows as "Pending" and does not count as offline.
notes.2: Search and quick commands: ⌘K / Ctrl+K.

nodes.list.title: Servers
nodes.list.intro: A server is your VPS with its own domain, running the proxy. The panel installs everything it needs with one command and then manages it through an agent: keys, cover site, restarts. One panel, any number of servers in different countries; a key can be bound to several at once.

status.name: Status
status.what: "Online" - the agent sent a heartbeat recently. "Offline" - no heartbeat for longer than the offline threshold (Settings → Notifications and polling). "Degraded" - the server answers but one of its services is down. "Pending" - the server was created, but the install command has not been run yet.

engine.name: Engine
engine.what: telemt - a single process that gives keys two links (WEB and Fake-TLS), per-key limits and per-key stats. tproxy - the older tproxy-server + MTProxy pair, WEB links only. Chosen when the server is created and fixed afterwards.

relay.name: Relay
relay.what: The proxy process version on the server: the telemt version or a short tproxy-server commit hash. Empty - the server has not reported yet.

profiles.name: Profiles
profiles.what: Used / maximum. A profile is one key on this server. A server has 128 slots by default; once they run out, new keys cannot be bound to it.

online.name: Online
online.what: An estimate of the people on the server right now, with its connections under it. A personal user with at least one connection is one person, a shared user counts as many as its distinct IP addresses; tproxy servers count WEB sessions. A dash means the server is offline or has sent nothing in the last three minutes.

load.name: CPU and RAM
load.what: Processor and memory load from the last heartbeat. Yellow from 80 %, red from 95 %. Keep headroom: an overloaded server adds latency for every client.

telegram.name: Telegram
telegram.what: Latency to Telegram from the last heartbeat - telemt's one figure across all datacenters. Yellow from 150 ms, red from 400. A dash on tproxy servers and on offline servers. Per-DC detail is on the server page, Overview tab.

heartbeat.name: Last response
heartbeat.what: When the agent last checked in. "never connected" - the install has not run, or the script did not reach registration.

changes.name: Changes
changes.what: The "pending" tag means the panel holds changes (new or revoked keys, a different site) not yet sent to the server. They go out on the next apply, or right away with "Apply now".

actions.name: Actions
actions.what: "Apply now" - send the accumulated changes now. "Install command" - mint a new one-time token and show the command (the old command stops working). "Delete" - remove the server together with its profiles and bindings. Keys bound only to this server are left with no servers.

notes.1: Applies run on their own every "How often to apply changes" (45 seconds by default). On a tproxy server every apply restarts the relay and drops live sessions; on a telemt server key changes go through the API without a restart.
notes.2: Servers and the panel must be separate servers: the proxy on a server takes ports 80 and 443.
notes.3: A server that stays "offline" usually cannot reach the panel's address (PANEL_PUBLIC_URL). On the VPS: journalctl -u tgwp-agent -n 100.

nodes.create.title: New server
nodes.create.intro: Here you describe the VPS that will become a panel server. The panel installs nothing yet: after creation it hands you one command to run on that server as root. Prepare the VPS first: clean Ubuntu 22.04+ or Debian 12+, a public IPv4, ports 80 and 443 free, and an A record for the domain that already points at this server.

name.name: Name
name.what: What the server is called in the panel and its lists. Any text, seen only by you and the other admins. Required.
name.tip: Name by location or provider: this is the name you pick servers by when issuing a key.

hostname.name: Host
hostname.what: The server's domain. The certificate is issued for it and every client link points at it. Lowercase letters, digits, hyphens and dots only; at least one dot; no https:// and no path; each part between dots is 1-63 characters and neither starts nor ends with a hyphen; 253 characters in total. Must be unique across servers.
hostname.tip: The A record for this domain must point at the server's IP BEFORE you run the install command: the script checks that first and cannot get a certificate without it.

engine.name: Engine
engine.what: telemt (default) - one process: clients get both a WEB link (through the server's site on 443) and a regular Fake-TLS link on a separate port; per-key quotas, speed limits and traffic. tproxy - the classic tproxy-server + MTProxy pair: WEB links only, no per-key limits, every apply restarts the relay. The engine cannot be changed later - only by reinstalling the server.
engine.tip: Unless you have a reason to pick tproxy, keep telemt: it covers every official Telegram client and its WEB mode is the same.

tls_domain.name: Fake-TLS domain
tls_domain.what: telemt only. The domain the Fake-TLS port masquerades as: to the ISP the client looks like an ordinary HTTPS connection to that site, and anyone probing the port without a secret sees the real site. Same spelling rules as the host. Defaults to the server's own host, and that is the right choice: it already has a real cover site and a valid certificate.
tls_domain.tip: A foreign domain only works if it is a real site answering HTTPS on port 443 with a valid certificate, and the server can reach it. A domain with no site on 443 breaks the masking: telemt takes the TLS fingerprint with a real connection and will not activate its config without one.

classic_port.name: Fake-TLS port
classic_port.what: telemt only. The port on which the server accepts classic MTProto (Fake-TLS) connections. 1024 to 65535; 80 and 443 belong to the server's web server. Default 8443.
classic_port.tip: The port must be open in the VPS firewall and at the provider. It is baked into every Fake-TLS link, so changing it later means reissuing links.

acme_email.name: E-mail for Let's Encrypt
acme_email.what: Contact address for certificate issuance: Let's Encrypt writes to it when a certificate fails to renew. Must be a valid address; it goes into the install script and Caddy's config on the server.

public_ip.name: Public IP
public_ip.what: The server's IPv4 address. Optional: a telemt server detects it during install. If set, the install script and "Check from the panel" compare the domain's A record against it.
public_ip.tip: Set it when the server has several addresses or sits behind NAT with a forwarded public IP - auto-detection may pick the wrong one there.

notes.1: The panel and the server are different servers. On the panel's server ports 80/443 are taken by the panel itself.
notes.2: Order: A record → create the server here → run the command on the VPS → a minute later the server is "online". If the record came later, just run the same command again.
notes.3: After install the server must be able to reach its own public address on port 443 (that is how Fake-TLS masking works). Check from the server itself: curl -sSI https://<server host>/ should return the site's response.

nodes.install.title: Install command
nodes.install.intro: The one line that turns a clean VPS into a panel server: installs the proxy, the Caddy web server and the agent, obtains a Let's Encrypt certificate and registers the server in the panel. Run it on the VPS as root; it usually takes a minute or two.

command.name: Command
command.what: curl downloads a personal script by one-time token and pipes it into bash. Copy it whole and paste into the server's terminal (SSH as root, or via sudo).

expires.name: Valid until
expires.what: The token lives 24 hours and is spent exactly once - at the registration step. If it has expired, open the server and press "Show install command": the panel mints a new one.

preflight.name: Pre-flight checks
preflight.what: The script first checks: x86_64, systemd, that the panel is reachable from this server, the public IP, that the domain's A record points here, and that ports 80, 443 and the Fake-TLS port are free. A failed DNS or ports check shows a menu: [r] re-run, [c] continue anyway, [q] quit.
preflight.tip: The most common stop is an A record that has not propagated yet or points elsewhere. Fix the record in another window and press r.

installs.name: What gets installed
installs.what: For telemt: the pinned telemt binary (sha256 verified), Caddy for TLS on 443, the tgwp-agent, the cover site, nftables rules, network sysctls (BBR, short keepalives). For tproxy: the pinned tproxy-server commit, the official MTProxy, Caddy and the agent. The script then waits up to two minutes for https://<host>/ to answer with a valid certificate and only then registers the server.

regenerate.name: Running it again
regenerate.what: If the script failed before the "Registration" step (usually while waiting for the certificate), fix the cause and run the same command again: installed packages are reused and the token is still unspent. "Show install command" on the server page mints a new token, and the previous command stops working.

notes.1: Server requirements: clean Ubuntu 22.04+ or Debian 12+, x86_64, root, public IPv4, ports 80 and 443 free. The script does not touch the firewall - open the ports yourself (for telemt, the Fake-TLS port too).
notes.2: Without a terminal (a cloud console that just runs the script) a failed check makes it exit. To continue anyway: curl … | sudo TGWP_SKIP_PREFLIGHT=1 bash.
notes.3: The error message ends with the last 30 lines of the Caddy or telemt journal - the answer is usually there.

nodes.check.title: Check from the panel
nodes.check.intro: From its own side, the panel walks the same steps a Telegram client takes when connecting: resolve the domain, knock on the ports, verify the certificate and the site. Run it after install, after a DNS change, and whenever "the server is online but clients cannot connect".

dns_a.name: DNS record
dns_a.what: The server's domain resolves to an IP address. If the server has a public IP set, the record must point exactly there. Fails when the record is missing, not propagated yet, or points at another server.

tcp_80.name: Port 80 (HTTP)
tcp_80.what: The port is open from outside. Let's Encrypt needs it to issue and renew the certificate. A failure is usually the VPS or provider firewall.

tcp_443.name: Port 443 (HTTPS)
tcp_443.what: The port is open from outside - both the cover site and the clients' WEB connections go through it. If it is closed, the remaining probes are skipped.

tls_cert.name: TLS certificate
tls_cert.what: Port 443 presents a valid certificate for the server's domain. Fails when Caddy could not obtain one (most often DNS or port 80) or it has expired.

pq_kex.name: Post-quantum key exchange
pq_kex.what: Informational: whether Caddy on the server negotiates hybrid X25519MLKEM768 with modern clients. Does not affect the overall result.

http_root.name: Site responds
http_root.what: GET https://<host>/ returns the cover site's page. Without a working site the traffic to the server does not look like ordinary HTTPS - which is the whole point of the disguise.

mask.name: Fake-TLS masking
mask.what: telemt only. The panel connects to the Fake-TLS port with the site name from "Fake-TLS domain" and no secret - as a prober would - and expects to see that domain's real certificate. A failure means the server cannot reach <Fake-TLS domain>:443 (port closed, a domain with no site, or the server not allowed to connect to its own public address).
mask.tip: From the server itself: curl -sSI https://<Fake-TLS domain>/ must return the site's response. If it does not, the problem is the VPS network, not the panel.

notes.1: The check runs from the panel's server. If the panel has its own egress firewall, some probes will fail even though clients work fine.
notes.2: A red line with the detail "expected 203.0.113.10" means the A record does not point at the public IP set in the panel: fix either the record or the IP on the server.

nodes.detail.title: Server page
nodes.detail.intro: Everything about one server on five tabs. A tproxy server has no Settings tab. "Apply changes" in the header sends the accumulated changes without waiting for the next cycle.

header.name: Header
header.what: Status dot, name, domain with a copy button and tags: the telemt or relay version, the Fake-TLS port (domain:port when it masks behind another domain) and the agent version.

apply.name: Apply changes
apply.what: Send the accumulated changes to the server now. The panel applies them on its own about once a minute anyway (set under Settings → Notifications and polling). On a telemt server keys go through the API without a restart; on a tproxy server the relay restarts and live sessions drop.

tab_overview.name: Health
tab_overview.what: At the top, what is wrong, if anything. Below, a line of key numbers: status, people online (click it for this server's users), processor and memory, latency to Telegram and the result of the checks. Under it, people online, processor and traffic over a day or a week, and rows that open on click: Telegram datacenters, Services, Server checks and WEB transport. Each row says in a few words how things are, and a row with a problem is already open. "Check now" runs the full check and the check from the panel.

tab_settings.name: Settings
tab_settings.what: The Fake-TLS address, port and domains, the public IP and the sponsor channel tag. Below, the WEB transport strategy and reliability with the route to Telegram are folded away, each row showing the current choice. Changing the Fake-TLS domain or port breaks links already handed out; nothing else does.

tab_site.name: Cover site
tab_site.what: Which site an ordinary visitor of the server domain sees, a preview and a template switch. A new site reaches the server with the next apply.

tab_blocklist.name: Blocklist
tab_blocklist.what: Addresses and subnets the server refuses connections from. The list lives in the panel and returns to the server after a reboot or a reinstall.

tab_maintenance.name: Maintenance
tab_maintenance.what: The telemt and agent versions with the telemt update, actions (restart the proxy, the install command), the apply history and, set apart, deleting the server.

restart.name: Restart relay / telemt
restart.what: On the Maintenance tab. A forced restart of the proxy process; every current connection drops. Rarely needed: when the process hangs and the checks show the network is fine.

install.name: Show install command
install.what: On the Maintenance tab. Issues a new single-use token valid for 24 hours and shows the command. Use it to reinstall the agent or when the first install never reached registration. The old command stops working at once.

logs.name: Service logs
logs.what: The panel shows no logs: read them on the server itself over SSH. Ready-made commands for the agent, telemt, caddy and tproxy are in the "Server logs" section of docs/runbook.md.

delete.name: Delete server
delete.what: On the Maintenance tab. Removes the server from the panel together with its keys on it and bindings. The VPS itself is untouched: the proxy keeps running on the old configuration until you stop it. Keys bound only to this server are left without servers.

notes.1: While the server is not connected, the top of Health says what to check on the server itself, and the rows with live data stay empty.
notes.2: A yellow status on a running server usually means one service is down: open Services on Health and read that service's logs on the server.

nodes.listeners.title: Addresses and Fake-TLS
nodes.listeners.intro: The telemt server's public address and the settings of its classic MTProto port. The Fake-TLS domain and port are baked into every Fake-TLS link already handed out (the domain sits inside the secret), so changing them is not a setting - it is reissuing links: after saving, the next apply rewrites the config, restarts telemt, drops connections, and every Fake-TLS link of this server stops working. WEB links are unaffected. Changing the public IP restarts telemt too, but leaves the links alone.

tls_domain.name: Fake-TLS domain
tls_domain.what: The site the port masquerades as. The right choice is the server's own host: it has a real cover site and a certificate. A foreign domain is acceptable only if it is a real site answering HTTPS on 443 that the server can reach. Spelling rules as for the host: lowercase, with a dot, no scheme.
tls_domain.tip: After changing it, run "Check from the panel": the "Fake-TLS masking" line tells you whether the new domain works.

tls_domains.name: Backup masking domains
tls_domains.what: Extra domains the Fake-TLS port also masquerades as. Each one gives every key its own link, and the main link stays as it was. If a provider starts blocking the main domain by SNI, the user takes the link with another domain, with no need to reinstall the server. Saving restarts telemt but does not break links already handed out.
tls_domains.tip: Use real sites with HTTPS on 443 that the server can reach: telemt takes the TLS fingerprint of each domain at startup, and if one is unreachable the apply rolls back. Needs agent 2.9.2 or later.

classic_port.name: Fake-TLS port
classic_port.what: 1024 to 65535, except 80 and 443 (taken by Caddy). Must be open in the firewall. Default 8443.

public_ip.name: Public IP
public_ip.what: The IPv4 address the server is reachable at from the internet. telemt names it in the WEB vhost (public_addr) and "Check from the panel" compares the host's A record against it. The install script detects it and reports it at registration; correct it here when it picked the wrong one.
public_ip.tip: It must be the address the A record points at. On a NAT host the interface address and the one the internet sees can differ - the installer shows both; "connection refused" on 80/443 means the wrong one is recorded.

notes.1: Change these only as a last resort, and plan to send new links to everyone holding a Fake-TLS link of this server. Subscription pages update on their own.
notes.2: Saving only records the intent: the next apply (automatic, or the "Apply now" button) sends it to the server.

nodes.dcs.title: Telegram datacenters
nodes.dcs.intro: How the server sees Telegram's datacenters: the state of the direct route to them and the latency to each DC. The figures are not the panel's but telemt's own: it keeps a moving average of the latency to every DC and refreshes it with its own health checks. telemt servers only; tproxy does not report this.

route.name: Route
route.what: The line above the table: the kind of route (the panel's is always direct), how many connections to Telegram succeeded out of all attempts, and how long ago telemt last checked the route. The dot beside it is the route's tone: green when all is well; yellow when the route is up but has been failing; red when telemt considers it down.

connections.name: Connections
connections.what: telemt's counters since it started: successful and failed attempts to connect to Telegram. A growing share of failures at normal latency usually means the network between the server and Telegram, not the server itself.

latency.name: Latency
latency.what: The moving average of the DC's response time in milliseconds over telemt's checks. Gray below 150 ms, yellow from 150, red from 400. A dash means the DC has not been measured yet.
latency.tip: A red DC does not mean the server is down: every user whose chats live in that DC feels the lag on this server. If it does not pass, move the keys to a server where that DC is green.

ip_preference.name: IP preference
ip_preference.what: Which address telemt chose for the DC, IPv4 or IPv6. It changes on its own from the check results; there is nothing to set by hand.

notes.1: This is latency from the server to Telegram, not to the user. A server with green DCs that is far from its users is still slow for them.
notes.2: "Not available on this engine" is a tproxy server. "telemt is not reporting datacenter data" means telemt older than 3.5.7, or its upstream checks are disabled in its config.

keys.list.title: Users
keys.list.intro: A user is access to the proxy for one person or for a group. Every user has a subscription link: the person opens it and connects the proxy step by step. Here you find, filter, open, turn off, extend and delete users, one at a time or in bulk.

chips.name: States above the list
chips.what: A row of buttons with counts: all users, active, expiring within 7 days, expired and turned off. Setting up and Revoked appear when there are any. The pressed button leaves only those in the list; All clears it.

state.name: State
state.what: "Active": access works. "Waiting to apply": the change has not reached the servers yet, usually under a minute. "Turned off": you paused the access. "Expired": the date has passed and access is off the servers, but it comes back when you extend the date. "Revoked": access is closed for good.

type.name: Type
type.what: Personal: one person's access, which you can turn off or revoke without touching anyone else. Shared: one link for a group; it is turned off or revoked for everyone at once.

columns.name: Columns
columns.what: The Columns button hides and shows columns: activity, expiry, traffic for 30 days, servers, type, link and creation date. The choice is remembered in this browser.
columns.tip: The Activity column shows whether the person is online and from about how many devices (distinct IP addresses), with their connections below; when offline, when they last connected. Only telemt servers count this.

search.name: Search and filters
search.what: Search by name, contact, note and short address. Filters narrows the list by type and server; an active filter shows next to the state buttons, and its cross removes it. A link like /users?node=<id> opens the users of one server, and /users?user=<id> opens one user.

open.name: User window
open.what: Click anywhere on a row: it lights up and shows an arrow at its end, and a click opens the user window. The checkbox, the copy button and the "…" menu on the row work on their own. The menu copies the subscription link, extends by a month, turns access off or on, and deletes the user.

pages.name: Pages
pages.what: Under the list it says which rows are shown, for example "Showing 26–50 of 132". Rows per page picks 25, 50 or 100, and the choice is remembered in this browser. The page number is in the address, so the browser's Back returns to the previous page. Changing a filter or the search goes back to the first page.

bulk.name: Bulk actions
bulk.what: Tick several rows: Extend sets one new date for all, Turn off and Turn on pause and resume access, Revoke access and Delete apply to all at once, up to 500 at a time. Deleting cannot be undone; revoking keeps the entry in the list.

notes.1: Changes reach people after the server applies them: on a schedule, every 45 seconds by default, or with Apply now on the server page. telemt applies without a restart, tproxy restarts its relay.
notes.2: A server has a limited number of places, 128 by default. When they run out, the panel refuses and names the server.
notes.3: Viewers see the list but not the links or secrets.

keys.create.title: New user
keys.create.intro: Three tabs, three ways to give access: One person, Shared access for a group on one link, and Several users at once. The subscription link is created automatically, and the user window opens afterwards so you can copy and send it right away.

tabs.name: Tabs
tabs.what: One person: personal access. Shared access: one link for a group; only shared access has a short address. Several: a series of personal users named prefix-1, prefix-2 and so on. Move in: people from another panel with their own secrets.

label.name: Name
label.what: What the user is called in the panel: the person's name or the group's. Required. Never shown to people or put in the link.
label.tip: You will search by it later: write it so that in a year you still know who it was for.

owner_label.name: Contact
owner_label.what: Optional. How to reach the person: Telegram username, phone or e-mail. The list search finds it.

sub_slug.name: Short address
sub_slug.what: Shared access only, optional. Instead of a long link you get a short one like …/s/team that is easy to dictate and remember. 3-32 characters: lowercase Latin letters, digits and dashes, not starting or ending with a dash.

expires_at.name: Access until
expires_at.what: No end date by default. Untick it and pick a date, or press +1 month, +3 months or +1 year. When the date passes, access is taken off the servers, and extending the date brings it back.

nodes.name: Servers
nodes.what: Tick at least one. The subscription page shows the person every ticked server. Next to each server you see how many places are taken; a full server cannot be picked.
nodes.tip: You can add or remove servers later in the user window.

carrier_mode.name: Transport
carrier_mode.what: Chosen automatically on telemt servers. A mode is only picked for legacy tproxy servers: HTTPS is the most compatible, WebSocket is faster, and the "lanes" variants open a separate connection per stream.
carrier_mode.tip: On tproxy start with HTTPS and change it only if people report slowness or drops.

limits.name: Limits
limits.what: Traffic quota, speed, number of IP addresses and connections. telemt enforces them, so they are available when a telemt server is among the chosen ones. tproxy servers have Additional limits. An empty field means no limit.

note.name: Note
note.what: Free text for you and your colleagues: who asked, what is paid until when. Never shown to people and never on the subscription page.

notes.1: A new user starts working once the server applies the change, usually within a minute.
notes.2: On a telemt server a user has two direct links, WEB and Fake-TLS; on a tproxy server only WEB. The subscription page picks the one that fits the device.

keys.transport.title: Transport
keys.transport.intro: How the person's Telegram talks to the server. On telemt this belongs to the server and the network, not to the user: nothing is pinned to a particular person.

automatic.name: Automatic choice
automatic.what: On telemt servers the transport is negotiated per connection. The server tries the options in order and remembers what worked on that network, so there is nothing to choose in the user window.
automatic.tip: If someone sees slow or dropping connections, look at the server and the network: start from the server check.

order.name: Negotiation order
order.what: Fastest first, most compatible last. Once an option works, the server remembers it instead of walking the list again for every connection.
order.example: WebSocket lanes → WebSocket → HTTPS lanes → HTTPS

legacy.name: Legacy tproxy servers
legacy.what: tproxy negotiates nothing, so its carrier mode is set here and goes into the profile on the server. With servers of both engines selected, only the tproxy ones get the mode.
legacy.tip: For tproxy start with HTTPS and change it only if users complain about speed or drops.

notes.1: None of this affects the Fake-TLS link: telemt only, and it works differently.

keys.batch.title: Several users
keys.batch.intro: Creates several personal users with the same settings: servers, expiry, limits. Names follow the pattern prefix-number. Handy when you hand out access one per person and do not know the names yet. The panel checks that every server has room and creates either all of them or none.

prefix.name: Prefix
prefix.what: Required. The start of every user's name; a dash and a number are added.

count.name: Count
count.what: From 1 to 100 at a time. Each takes one place on every chosen server.

result.name: Result
result.what: Afterwards the panel lists the users, each with a button to copy the subscription link and Open. Download all links gives a text file: subscription links first, one line per person, then the direct links per server.

notes.1: If a server has fewer places than users in the series, the panel refuses the whole series and names the server. Lower the count or drop the server.
notes.2: Users from a series are ordinary users: you can rename, turn off or extend them one by one later.

keys.import.title: Move users in
keys.import.intro: Brings people over from another panel or proxy together with their secrets, so the links they have in Telegram stay the same. Everyone gets the same settings: servers, expiry, limits. The panel checks every line and the room on each server and creates either all of them or none.

list.name: List
list.what: Paste an export from the old panel, the [access.users] section of a telemt config, or plain links. Empty lines and lines starting with # or [ are skipped. Below the box you see what the panel made of each line.

name.name: Name
name.what: Whatever comes before the secret. Without a name, as with a bare link, the panel names the user after the start of the secret; you can rename later. Text after the secret becomes the contact.

secret.name: Secret
secret.what: 32 hex characters. From links prefixed with ee or dd the panel takes the secret out itself, and from ee links the masking domain too. A secret another panel user already has, or one repeated in the list, is refused.

move.name: Moving
move.what: Old links point at the old address and port. Point that address at the new server, keep the port, and make the masking domain of the old Fake-TLS links the server's main or backup domain.

notes.1: Up to 500 people at a time. Each takes a place on every chosen server.
notes.2: Once moved they are ordinary users: you can rename, turn off or extend them, or give them a new secret.

keys.limits.title: User limits
keys.limits.intro: Two sets of ceilings. The first five are enforced by telemt on the server - they work only on telemt servers and change without a restart. The rest are WEB-transport ceilings on sessions and streams, enforced by the relay. An empty field or 0 always means no limit (for the WEB-transport ones: the server's default).

quota_gb.name: Traffic quota, GB
quota_gb.what: Total traffic the user may transfer, up plus down. A gigabyte here is 1024³ bytes, as in the Traffic column. Once the quota is used up, telemt stops serving the user. Maximum 100 TB, as a typo guard.

rate_up_mbit.name: Upload speed, Mbit/s
rate_up_mbit.what: Speed ceiling from the client to Telegram's servers. A megabit here is 1,000,000 bits per second, as in ISP plans. 10 Mbit/s ≈ 1.25 MB/s.

rate_down_mbit.name: Download speed, Mbit/s
rate_down_mbit.what: Speed ceiling from Telegram to the client - that is media and file downloads. 20-50 Mbit/s is usually enough for comfortable video.

max_unique_ips.name: Max unique IPs
max_unique_ips.what: From how many different IP addresses the access may be used at the same time. A simple way to keep shared access from spreading across the internet. Up to 1,000,000.
max_unique_ips.tip: One person on a phone with mobile data changes IP often; give personal access at least 3-5. For shared access the limit has to be at least the number of people in the group.

max_tcp_conns.name: Max connections
max_tcp_conns.what: How many TCP connections the user may hold open at once. A Telegram client opens several per device. Up to 1,000,000.

max_sessions.name: Max sessions
max_sessions.what: How many WEB sessions (roughly devices) the user may have open at the same time.

max_streams.name: Max streams
max_streams.what: How many data streams (connections to Telegram's servers) the user may hold in total across all sessions.

max_streams_per_session.name: Max streams per session
max_streams_per_session.what: The same, per session. Cannot exceed "Max streams".

max_pending_per_session.name: Max pending per session
max_pending_per_session.what: How many streams of one session may be in the connecting stage at once.

max_backend_dials_in_flight.name: Max concurrent backend dials
max_backend_dials_in_flight.what: How many connections to Telegram's servers the relay may be opening for the user at the same time. Cannot exceed "Max streams".

new_sessions_per_minute.name: New sessions / min
new_sessions_per_minute.what: Rate limit: how many new sessions per minute may be opened. Protection against a leaked link that hundreds of clients try to use.

new_sessions_burst.name: New sessions burst
new_sessions_burst.what: How many sessions may open in one burst above the per-minute rate - say, when the whole team connects at once in the morning.

new_streams_per_minute.name: New streams / min
new_streams_per_minute.what: As for sessions, but for data streams.

new_streams_burst.name: New streams burst
new_streams_burst.what: The allowed burst of new streams above the per-minute rate.

notes.1: If the user is only on tproxy servers, the telemt limits are shown greyed out: nothing enforces them. They start working as soon as you add a telemt server.
notes.2: The WEB-transport limits are fine tuning. Leave zeros until you have a specific problem: a server's own defaults handle ordinary load.
notes.3: Every limit change reaches the server on the next apply.

keys.detail.title: User window
keys.detail.intro: Everything about one user in one window with four tabs. Main holds what you send to the person and the basic fields; the others hold access, limits and statistics. Save at the bottom saves every tab at once, servers included; changes reach the servers at the next apply.

header.name: Header
header.what: Name, state, type, contact and whether the person is online: "Online, ≈ 2 devices" or when they were last seen. On the Main tab the panel says when access is waiting to apply, turned off, expired or revoked. A revoked user opens read-only.

overview.name: Main
overview.what: The "Access is on" switch and four facts: expiry (red once it has passed, amber with less than a week left), traffic for 30 days, on how many of all servers the user is, and when they were last online. The creation date is at the bottom of the tab.

subscription.name: Subscription link
subscription.what: The main thing you send: one link to all of the person's servers; on its page they pick their device and connect step by step. The link is always visible: copy it, show the QR code or open the page to see what the person sees. Shared access with a short address shows the short link, with the full one below.
subscription.tip: If the window says the link cannot be shown, it was made before the panel update. Press Issue a new link; the old one then stops opening.

direct_links.name: Direct links
direct_links.what: The "Direct proxy links" row, with the number of links, opens t.me and tg:// links and QR codes for each server, WEB and Fake-TLS. They are useful when the person prefers not to use the subscription page.

about.name: About the user and expiry
about.what: Name, contact and note; shared access also has its short address. Below is the expiry with +1 month, +3 months, +1 year or No end date. The buttons extend from the current end date, or from today if that date has already passed.

access.name: Access and servers
access.what: The access type (chosen at creation and fixed), the servers as checkboxes in the same order as the server list, and the transport when some of the servers run tproxy.

limits.name: Limits
limits.what: Traffic quota, speed, and the number of IP addresses and connections for telemt servers, plus the extended limits for tproxy. An empty field means no limit.

stats.name: Statistics
stats.what: Connections right now, traffic over 24 hours or 7 days, and a chart for each server. Only telemt servers count these.

save.name: Save
save.what: Becomes active once you change something. If a field does not pass the check, the window switches to the tab with that field and marks the tab. If you close the window without saving, the panel offers the draft back next time.

manage.name: More actions → Manage
manage.what: Turn off pauses access, Turn on brings it back. Change secret replaces the direct links while the subscription link stays the same: the person opens it and presses Connect again. New subscription link replaces the link, and the old one stops opening.
manage.tip: If a link reached the wrong people, issue a new subscription link and change the secret.

danger.name: More actions → Danger zone
danger.what: Revoke access closes access for good; the user stays in the list for the record. Delete removes the user, their links and statistics. For a pause use Turn off.

notes.1: Traffic and activity are counted only by telemt servers; on tproxy these values stay empty.
notes.2: While the state is Waiting to apply, the link is already shown but starts working after the server applies it, usually within a minute.

keys.link.title: Direct links
keys.link.intro: With a direct link the person enables the proxy in Telegram with one tap. The window shows one block per server of the user. It is usually simpler to send the single subscription link from the user window: its page gathers every server and the steps for each device.

web.name: WEB
web.what: A link of the form https://t.me/webproxy?server=<host>&secret=<secret>. The client goes through the server's site on port 443 - plain HTTPS to the network. Available on every server. Client support: Telegram Desktop stable, Android experimental, iOS not yet.

fake_tls.name: Fake-TLS
fake_tls.what: A link of the form https://t.me/proxy?server=<host>&port=<port>&secret=ee…. A classic MTProto proxy disguised as HTTPS; every official Telegram client on every platform understands it. telemt servers only; the port is the server's "Fake-TLS port".
fake_tls.tip: For iOS users and older clients hand out Fake-TLS.

tme_vs_tg.name: t.me and tg://
tme_vs_tg.what: The same thing in two forms. https://t.me/… opens from any browser or messenger and forwards into Telegram. tg://… is a direct link into the app; useful where t.me is blocked, but not clickable in some chats.

qr.name: QR code
qr.what: The same link as an image: show it on screen or put it in a guide. The Telegram client on a phone opens it via the camera scanner. "Download QR" saves a PNG.

clients.name: On the user's side
clients.what: Open the link → Telegram asks "Enable proxy?" → Connect. Verify: Settings → Data and Storage → Proxy. If the proxy will not connect, check the server's "Prerequisite check" first.

notes.1: While the state is Waiting to apply, the link does not work yet: wait for the apply, usually under a minute.
notes.2: The link contains the secret: whoever sees it can connect. If it leaked, use More actions → Change secret in the user window.

keys.extend.title: Extend access
keys.extend.intro: Sets one new end date for every selected user. Handy when a group has paid for another month.

expires_at.name: New end date
expires_at.what: A date and time in your time zone, in the future. Replaces the previous date for every selected user, including those without one.

notes.1: You can extend users whose access has already expired: it comes back after the next apply.
notes.2: Revoked users cannot be extended.

sites.templates.title: Site templates
sites.templates.intro: Every server's domain must serve an ordinary, plausible website: to the ISP the proxy traffic then looks like visits to a site, and anyone opening the address sees a page rather than an error. A template is such a site: HTML plus files. The panel deploys a preset when a server is installed; here you pick another or write your own.

template.name: Template
template.what: A card with the name, a "Preset" tag for built-in ones and the last change. Click the name to open the editor.

preset.name: Preset
preset.what: Built-in templates. They cannot be deleted or renamed, but can be assigned to servers and duplicated as your own.

duplicate.name: Duplicate as own
duplicate.what: Makes a copy under your name - the usual way to start your own site from a working base.

delete.name: Delete
delete.what: Own templates only. Servers that already run it keep showing it until another one is assigned.

assign.name: Assign to server
assign.what: In the editor - the "Assign to server…" button; on the server page - the "Cover site" tab. Every server gets a uniquified copy: block order, class and file names differ, so servers do not share a signature.

notes.1: A template is at most 2 MB including files: it travels to the server inside every apply.
notes.2: A good template is boring: a small business card site, a personal page, documentation. Do not copy well-known sites.

sites.editor.title: Template editor
sites.editor.intro: HTML and files on the left, preview and validation on the right. The cover site lives on the server and must be fully self-contained: the relay forbids anything that pulls external resources or sends data out - otherwise the site would give the server away.

name.name: Template name
name.what: How the template appears in the list and in the server page's selector. A preset's name cannot be changed.

html.name: HTML
html.what: One whole page. Write styles and scripts right in <style> and <script> - on save the panel moves them into separate files. Not allowed: references to external resources (foreign CSS, fonts, images, scripts), inline handlers such as onclick, forms. Add images and fonts under "Files" and reference them by relative path.

assets.name: Files
assets.what: Images, fonts, extra CSS/JS. A file's path is how you reference it from the HTML. Total template size with the HTML: up to 2 MB.

validate.name: Validate
validate.what: Runs the same checks as saving and lists the violations with what exactly to remove. A save with errors is refused.

preview.name: Preview
preview.what: The page in a sandboxed frame - what a visitor to the server's domain sees. Check for broken images: they are the first sign of external references.

save.name: Save
save.what: Stores the template in the panel. Servers it is assigned to receive the new version on the next apply.

notes.1: An unfinished template is kept as a draft and offered back next time you open it.
notes.2: Common offenders: Google Fonts, CDN scripts, analytics counters, <form>. Replace with local files or remove.

sites.assign.title: Assign template to server
sites.assign.intro: Pick a server and this template becomes its cover site. The panel marks the server as having pending changes; the site reaches the server on the next apply.

node.name: Server
node.what: The server the template is assigned to. It gets its own uniquified copy: file and class names differ from other servers with the same template.

notes.1: On a tproxy server the apply restarts the relay and drops live sessions; on a telemt server a site change also goes through an apply.
notes.2: The current template and its deployment status are on the server page → "Cover site" tab.

monitoring.title: Monitoring
monitoring.intro: Charts per server over the chosen range. Values come from stats snapshots the panel takes from the servers regularly, so a line can trail "now" by a few minutes. Metrics export for Prometheus and Grafana is under Settings → Integrations.

range.name: Range
range.what: 1 hour, 6 hours, 24 hours or 7 days. The longer the range, the coarser the averaging step.

people.name: People online
people.what: In the summary, how many people are online across all servers at once: someone connected to two servers counts once. On a telemt server's chart, how many people were on that server. A personal user with at least one connection is one person; a shared user counts as many as its distinct IP addresses. History recorded before this panel version has no such line.

sessions.name: Live sessions
sessions.what: tproxy only. How many client WEB sessions were open on the server at each moment. This is not an exact head count: depending on the client, one device may hold more than one session. tproxy reports nothing finer, so the panel counts people on such a server by its sessions.

streams.name: Live streams
streams.what: Connections to Telegram's servers inside the sessions. Usually several times the sessions; a sharp rise at the same session count is a sign of one key being abused.

traffic.name: Traffic
traffic.what: The server's outbound and inbound traffic over the range. Useful to see when a server will hit its VPS plan's cap.

connections.name: Connections (telemt)
connections.what: On telemt servers, the TCP connections telemt itself counts are shown instead of sessions and streams. One Telegram app holds several connections at once, usually 2 to 15, so there are more of them than people.

notes.1: A server with no data for the range was either just installed or offline: snapshots are taken from online servers only.
notes.2: Per-key statistics are in the key's drawer (telemt only).

audit.title: Activity log
audit.intro: Who did what and when in the panel: logins, key creation and revocation, server, settings and branding changes. The panel writes the entries itself; they cannot be edited or deleted from the UI. Use it to trace where a change came from and who issued a key.

action.name: Action
action.what: Filter by action group: login, admins, servers, keys, templates, branding, settings, alerts.

user.name: User
user.what: The admin's username. "system" - the panel itself acted: an automatic apply, an expiry revocation, an alert.

dates.name: From / To
dates.what: Range bounds in your time zone. Empty - unbounded.

target.name: Target
target.what: What was touched: the id of a key, server, template or profile.

ip.name: IP
ip.what: The address the request came from. Behind a reverse proxy the panel takes it from X-Forwarded-For.

details.name: Details
details.what: Extra fields of the entry: the key name, what exactly changed, the result of a test message. Opened with "Details".

notes.1: Secrets and passwords never reach the log - only the fact of the action.
notes.2: Entries are part of the database backup like everything else.

settings.panel.title: Server polling
settings.panel.intro: Two numbers that decide how fast the panel reacts. Only the owner can change them; the values from .env (APPLY_INTERVAL, OFFLINE_AFTER) are the initial ones, overridden here without a restart.

apply_interval.name: How often to apply changes, s
apply_interval.what: How often the worker checks the servers for unsent changes and sends them. 10 to 3600 seconds, default 45. A key created in the panel starts working no later than this interval.
apply_interval.tip: On tproxy servers every apply restarts the relay. If keys are issued often, a longer interval (120-300) means fewer restarts - the changes simply pile into one batch.

offline_after.name: Offline after, s
offline_after.what: How many seconds without an agent heartbeat the panel waits before calling the server offline and raising an alert. 30 to 3600, default 90.
offline_after.tip: Too small a threshold gives false alerts on any network hiccup; do not go below 60.

notes.1: "Apply now" on a server and "Apply everywhere" in the command palette do not wait for the interval.

settings.telegram.title: Telegram notifications
settings.telegram.intro: The panel messages Telegram when a server goes offline or comes back and when an apply on a server fails. You need your own bot and a chat for it to write to.

enabled.name: Enable notifications
enabled.what: The master switch. The token and chat id are kept when it is off.

bot_token.name: Bot token
bot_token.what: Create a bot with @BotFather (the /newbot command) and copy the token from its reply. The panel stores the token encrypted and never shows it again - the field only replaces it. "Token set" means one exists.

chat_id.name: Chat ID
chat_id.what: Where to write. For direct messages - your numeric id (ask @userinfobot); send your bot /start first, or it cannot message you. For a group - its id, a negative number; supergroups start with -100. Add the bot to the group.

test.name: Send a test message
test.what: Sends a probe with the token and chat id as typed, without saving them. If it arrives, save. The test result is written to the activity log.

language.name: Notification language
language.what: Every Telegram notification, the test message included, arrives in the chosen language: Russian or English. The panel interface does not change.

notes.1: "chat not found" - the bot cannot write to this chat: you never pressed /start in the DM, or the bot is not in the group.
notes.2: "unauthorized" - the token is wrong or was revoked in @BotFather.

settings.integrations.title: Integrations
settings.integrations.intro: What connects the panel to other systems. These settings live in the panel's .env file, so the tab shows what is already on and how to turn on the rest.

prometheus.name: Metrics export
prometheus.what: The panel serves its metrics at /metrics in the Prometheus text format: servers and users by state, live sessions and people online. You can copy a Prometheus scrape job straight from the tab.

token.name: METRICS_TOKEN
token.what: A token from the panel's .env. Prometheus sends it in the Authorization: Bearer header. Without it /metrics is open to anyone, and the tab warns about that.

node_metrics.name: Server metrics
node_metrics.what: One server's relay metrics are served at /api/v1/nodes/{id}/metrics. That address needs a panel sign-in, so Prometheus does not collect it.

grafana.name: Grafana dashboard
grafana.what: A ready dashboard is in the repository at deploy/grafana/tgwp-panel.json. Import it into Grafana and pick your Prometheus data source.

webhook.name: Alert webhook
webhook.what: The panel can send the same alerts that go to Telegram as a POST to your HTTPS endpoint. The endpoint and the secret are set in .env as ALERT_WEBHOOK_URL and ALERT_WEBHOOK_SECRET, and the panel needs a restart afterwards.
webhook.tip: Check the X-TGWP-Signature on your side and drop requests older than five minutes.

settings.security.title: Password and 2FA
settings.security.intro: Your account's password and second factor. The panel is the one place from which access to every server can be issued, so right after install change the password and turn on two-factor authentication.

password.name: Change password
password.what: Current password, new one (at least 10 characters) and its repeat. After the change every other session of this account is ended - other devices have to log in again.

totp.name: Two-factor authentication
totp.what: One-time codes from an authenticator app (Google Authenticator, Aegis, 1Password and any other TOTP app). To enable: scan the QR code or type the key by hand, enter the code the app shows and your password. The section is hidden when the panel's .env has FEATURE_TOTP=false.

recovery.name: Recovery codes
recovery.what: Eight one-time codes the panel shows exactly once - right after enabling. Each stands in for an app code once. Save them in a password manager before closing the dialog.

disable.name: Disable
disable.what: Requires the password and a current code. Afterwards the password alone logs you in and the recovery codes are deleted.

notes.1: Lost both the app and the recovery codes: the owner resets 2FA on the panel's server with docker compose exec panel /app/panel admin totp-reset <username>.
notes.2: "Invalid code" with the right app is almost always a phone clock that drifted. Turn on automatic time.

settings.admins.title: Admins
settings.admins.intro: Accounts that can log in to the panel. Only the owner creates and deletes them. Give every person their own account - then the activity log says who did what.

username.name: Username
username.what: At least 2 characters, unique. Cannot be changed later - only a new account can be created.

password.name: Password
password.what: At least 10 characters. Tell it to the person and ask them to change it right away under Settings → Password and 2FA.

role.name: Role
role.what: Owner - everything, including panel settings, admins and backups. Admin - servers, keys, templates and branding, but not panel settings or accounts. Viewer - read only: no key links or secrets.

notes.1: The last owner cannot be deleted, nor can you delete your own account.
notes.2: The first account is created by the installer or by panel admin create on the server - the same way you add an owner if all access is lost.

settings.branding.title: Appearance
settings.branding.intro: How the panel looks to admins and to users on the subscription page: name, logo, colours, texts. Settings are grouped into profiles; the active profile applies to everyone at once, no rebuild. It is handy to keep a "live" and a "draft" profile and switch.

profiles.name: Profiles
profiles.what: "Create from active" copies the current settings and files under a new name. "Activate" turns a profile on for everyone. Any profile but the active one can be deleted. Unsaved changes are lost when switching profiles - the panel asks first.

panel_name.name: Panel name
panel_name.what: Shown in the browser tab, the sidebar, the login page and the Telegram test message.

logo.name: Logo
logo.what: PNG, JPEG, ICO or SVG up to 2 MB. SVG is stripped of scripts. Shown in the sidebar and on the login page. Empty - the built-in mark.

favicon.name: Favicon
favicon.what: The browser-tab icon, same formats and limit. Best square, 32×32 or SVG.

login_bg.name: Login background
login_bg.what: The image on the left half of the login page. Empty - the brand pattern.

primary_color.name: Primary colour
primary_color.what: The primary button and first chart-series color. Links, focus and active navigation use theme-adjusted shades for readability. Accepts #rgb or #rrggbb.

accent_color.name: Accent colour
accent_color.what: The second chart series and secondary accents. #rgb or #rrggbb. Pick one distinguishable from the primary and from the green/yellow/red status colours.

theme_default.name: Default theme
theme_default.what: Dark or light - for people who have not switched the theme themselves. A user's own choice is stored in their browser and wins.

login_text.name: Login page text
login_text.what: A short message under the "Sign in" heading: who the panel is for, where to ask for access.

support_link.name: Support link
support_link.what: Empty, or an address starting with http:// or https://. Shown on the login page and the subscription page.

footer_text.name: Footer text
footer_text.what: The line at the bottom of the login page and the subscription page: company name, year.

custom_css.name: Custom CSS
custom_css.what: Your styles on top of the theme. The panel strips dangerous fragments (external imports, expressions, scripts) and reports what it removed. Fonts and images from foreign domains cannot be loaded from here.

personal.name: Personal preferences
personal.what: Theme (light, dark or system), density and sidebar state are saved in this browser. They do not change other users’ appearance. Reset restores the project theme, comfortable density and expanded sidebar.

logo_dark.name: Dark theme logo
logo_dark.what: Optional logo variant for a dark background. Used in navigation and on the login page; falls back to the main logo when not uploaded. The same formats and size limit apply.

notes.1: Preview name, colors and CSS directly in the interface; wide screens also show a separate preview. Save commits these fields. Images save immediately after upload. Shared changes affect everyone only for the active profile.
notes.2: Check contrast: brand-coloured text on the dark ground must stay readable (aim for at least 4.5:1).

settings.backups.title: Backups
settings.backups.intro: A backup is a dump of the whole panel database: servers, keys, secrets, settings, the activity log. Files live on the panel's server in the /data/backups/ volume. Owner only. Secrets in the dump stay encrypted with the MASTER_KEY from .env - without it a restored database is useless, so keep the key away from the server.

create.name: Create backup
create.what: Dumps right now without stopping the panel. Takes seconds; a second run while one is in progress is refused.

download.name: Download
download.what: Downloads the .dump file to your computer. Take copies off the server regularly: a backup on the same disk does not survive losing the server.

delete.name: Delete
delete.what: Removes the file from the panel's server. Copies you already downloaded stay with you.

schedule_enabled.name: Back up nightly
schedule_enabled.what: A daily scheduled backup. The oldest scheduled backups beyond the limit are deleted; manual ones are left alone.

schedule_hour.name: Time
schedule_hour.what: The hour to run, in UTC, 0 to 23. Pick the quietest time.

schedule_keep.name: Keep backups
schedule_keep.what: How many latest scheduled backups to keep, 1 to 60. 14 is two weeks of dailies.

restore.name: Restore
restore.what: Not done from the UI: on the panel's server stop the panel and run docker compose run --rm panel db restore /data/backups/<file>.dump --yes, then start the panel. Requires the same MASTER_KEY the backup was made with.

notes.1: Make a manual backup before upgrading the panel - the schedule never deletes it.
notes.2: Servers need no backup: the panel rebuilds their state with an apply after the database is restored.

settings.subscription.title: Subscription page
settings.subscription.intro: The public page a person opens from a subscription link: server cards with connect buttons, links and QR codes. Here you choose what it shows and in which words. The live preview is on the right.

language.name: Page language
language.what: "Browser language" by default: Russian for browsers set to Russian, Ukrainian, Belarusian or Kazakh, English for everyone else. Pick Russian or English to always open the page in it. Visitors can switch the language themselves either way.

title.name: Title and greeting
title.what: The text at the top of the page, separately for the Russian and English versions, since visitors can switch the language themselves. An empty field shows the standard text, which you see greyed out in it. Back to standard clears the field.

buttons.name: Buttons
buttons.what: The words on the Fake-TLS and WEB buttons, the lines under them and the support button's label. On every server the Fake-TLS button comes first and WEB second. Keep a mention that the WEB link does not work on iPhone in the line under it.

links.name: Which links to show
links.what: Fake-TLS works in every Telegram app, the WEB proxy only in Telegram Desktop and recent Android versions. Backup domains go into the server's Links and QR codes block.

blocks.name: What else to show
blocks.what: The access line under the title ("Access is active until …" or "Access never expires") and QR codes in the links block.

support.name: Support button
support.what: A button at the bottom of the page. Set its link here; an empty field falls back to the support link in Settings → Branding. Turned off, the button is not shown at all.

servers.name: Servers on the page
servers.what: An unticked server appears on no subscription page, but keys on it keep working. Handy for hiding a test or a spare server.

subscription.service.title: Subscription page service
subscription.service.intro: Subscription pages can open on a domain of your own instead of the panel's: people never see the panel's domain, and if you like, the pages run on a separate server. Until you set this up, pages open on the panel's domain.

where.name: Where pages open
where.what: "On the panel domain" keeps things as they were. "On my own domain" builds every link in the panel on the domain you enter. Old links on the panel domain redirect to the new one.

domain.name: Domain
domain.what: Just the domain, without a path. It must point at the panel server or the service server and serve HTTPS. Save it once the domain is up, or new links will not open for a while.

hide.name: Do not open pages on the panel domain
hide.what: By default old links on the panel domain redirect to the new domain. This box turns that off too: the panel domain is never shown, but old links stop working.

same_server.name: On the panel server
same_server.what: The second domain points at the panel server. install.sh --update --sub-domain adds it to the panel's Caddy and gets a certificate. On that domain the panel serves only subscription pages.

other_server.name: On another server
other_server.what: A small separate service without a database. "Get the install command" gives one command with a token: it installs Docker, the service and Caddy with a certificate for your domain. The service gets data from the panel with the token and keeps the last copy of each page.
other_server.tip: Ports 80 and 443 must be free on the new server, and it must reach the panel at the PANEL_PUBLIC_URL address.

status.name: Service status
status.what: Once a minute the service tells the panel it is online, with its version. If the version differs from the panel's, update the service with install.sh --subpage --update on its server.

notes.1: "New token" turns the old one off: run the new command on the service server afterwards.
notes.2: The preview in Subscription → Page always opens on the panel.

preferences.title: Personal preferences
preferences.description: Make the panel comfortable for you. These preferences are saved in this browser and do not change the appearance for other users.
preferences.project_description: The active profile’s name, images and colors are visible to everyone using the panel.

workspace.panel_settings_hint: Panel behavior, notifications and security. Configure proxy ports and transports on each server’s page.
workspace.settings_panel_hint: Refresh intervals and incident notifications. These settings apply to the entire panel.
workspace.settings_integrations_hint: How to connect the panel to other systems: metrics for Prometheus and Grafana, and alerts to your own endpoint.

reliability.maintenance_hint: Suspend automatic recovery and route switching.

reliability.apply_hint: Saving checks the new route and applies it on the server. The engine may need a restart, which interrupts active connections.

explain.a_record: The server's domain does not resolve in DNS. Proxy links don't work until it does.
explain.public_ip_match: The server's domain points at another IP address. Check the A record at your registrar.
explain.tcp_443: Port 443 on the server refuses connections. The cover site and the WEB proxy are unreachable.
explain.tls_handshake: The server did not complete a TLS handshake on port 443. Usually Caddy or the certificate is at fault.
explain.certificate: The site certificate does not match the server's domain, so HTTPS connections will be refused.
explain.certificate_expiry: The site certificate is about to expire or has expired. Caddy normally renews it itself. If not, check the Caddy log on the server.
explain.fake_tls_listener: The Fake-TLS port does not mask as the server's domain. Fake-TLS links may not work.
explain.https_response: The site on the server's domain answers unexpectedly, with a redirect or an error.
explain.decoy_site: The cover site returns an empty page. A stranger visiting the address sees nothing.
explain.caddy_service: The Caddy web server is not running. Without it the cover site and the WEB proxy are down.
explain.http2: The server did not negotiate HTTP/2. The WEB proxy still works, but slower.
explain.web_upstream: Caddy cannot pass requests to telemt, so the WEB proxy is down.
explain.carrier_failures: Some WEB proxy transports report failures. If there are many, the WEB link works poorly for some people.
explain.web_rejections: The proxy rejected some WEB connections. The reasons are under Server checks on the server's page.
explain.agent_link: The agent on the server did not answer the panel in time. This is usually a short network glitch. If it repeats, check that the server is reachable.
explain.service: The proxy service on the server is stopped, so nobody can connect.
explain.control_api: The proxy does not answer the panel's control API. Keys and settings won't apply until it does.
explain.readiness: The proxy is running but not ready to accept connections.
explain.tls_emulation: TLS emulation in the proxy is off, so Fake-TLS masks worse.
explain.tls_front_cache: The proxy could not capture the TLS profile of the masking domain. Fake-TLS may give itself away.
explain.tls_front_errors: TLS handshake failures are growing. Someone may be probing the server, or people have network trouble.
explain.upstream_health: The proxy cannot reach Telegram. People connect to the proxy, but messages don't go through.
explain.upstream_latency: The path from the server to Telegram is slow. Messages and media arrive late.
explain.datacenters: Some Telegram datacenters don't answer latency probes.
explain.connect_attempts: Some of the proxy's connections to Telegram failed in the last few minutes.
explain.dc_writers: The proxy keeps standing connections to every Telegram datacenter. This one has fewer than it needs, so some people may connect slowly or with errors. It usually recovers on its own.
explain.dc_down: There is no working connection to this Telegram datacenter. People whose accounts live there cannot use Telegram through this proxy.
explain.route: One of the routes to Telegram is down. The proxy tries the others.
explain.public_address: One of the domain's published addresses failed the TLS check or presents a certificate for another name.
explain.connection_failures: More than 20% of recent connections to Telegram failed.
explain.fd_pressure: telemt uses over 90% of its file descriptors and will soon stop accepting new connections.
explain.conntrack_pressure: The kernel connection tracking table is over 90% full. New connections may be dropped.
explain.inode_pressure: The disk is running out of inodes, the file entries, even if space remains.
explain.disk_pressure: The server's disk is at least 90% full.
explain.memory_pressure: The server's memory is at least 95% used.
explain.engine_unready: The proxy fails its readiness check, so people may not be able to connect.
explain.web_admission_closed: The proxy is not accepting new WEB sessions. This happens during an update or maintenance.
explain.probe_stale: The check from another network hasn't reported for a while. The check itself may be broken.
explain.probe_failed: The server failed a check from another network. It may be blocked there.

service.title: Subscription page service
service.hint: Where subscription pages open: on the panel's domain or on a separate domain, including on another server.
service.where_panel_hint: Subscription links look like https://{{host}}/s/…. Nothing else to set up.
service.domain_hint: Once saved, every link in the panel points at this domain, so set the domain up first in one of the ways on this page.
service.domain_invalid: Enter just a domain, for example sub.example.com, without a path.
service.domain_same_as_panel: The domain must differ from the panel's domain.
service.hide_on_panel: Do not open pages on the panel domain
service.hide_on_panel_off: Right now old links on {{host}} redirect to the new domain, so nothing breaks.
service.hide_on_panel_on: Pages on {{host}} stop opening altogether, and the panel domain is never shown. Old links on {{host}} stop working.
service.same_hint: The simplest way: the second domain points at the same server as the panel ({{host}}). The panel serves only subscription pages on it.
service.same_step_dns: Create an A record for {{domain}} pointing at the panel server's IP address.
service.same_step_save: Under "Where pages open", choose "On my own domain", enter the domain and save.
service.other_hint: Subscription pages run on a separate server, and the panel can stay hidden. The service keeps the last copy of each page, so pages open even while the panel is briefly unreachable.
service.command_once: The command contains the token and is shown only once. Copy it now.
service.other_step_dns: Create an A record for {{domain}} pointing at the new server's IP address.
service.other_step_save: Once the service is online, go to "Where pages open", choose "On my own domain", enter the domain and save.
service.reissue_description: The current token stops working. Run the new install command on the service server, or it loses contact with the panel.
service.revoke_description: The service stops getting data from the panel. Pages on its domain work from the saved copy for a while and then stop opening.

blocklist.title: Blocklist
blocklist.status_sending: On its way to the server, usually in under a minute
blocklist.status_waiting: The server is not connected: the list goes out as soon as it is back
blocklist.status_old_agent: The agent on this server cannot block addresses. Update it: on the server, as root, run tgwp-agent upgrade --agent. Only the agent restarts; people stay connected.
blocklist.status_error: The server did not apply the list: {{error}}
blocklist.dropped_total: Packets dropped since the list last changed: {{packets}} ({{bytes}})
blocklist.dropped_hint: Packets dropped since the list last changed
blocklist.add_hint: One per line: IPv4 or IPv6, a single address or a network such as 198.51.100.0/24. A note may follow the address after a space.
blocklist.how_it_works: The server drops everything coming from these addresses, connections already open included. Replies to connections the server opened itself (to the panel and to Telegram) always get through. Do not add your own address: you would not be able to reach the server over SSH from it either.
blocklist.empty: The list is empty. Add an address when it guesses secrets, scans the server or loads it for nothing.
blocklist.saved: List saved and in force on the server
blocklist.saved_waiting: List saved; it goes to the server once the server is connected
blocklist.saved_not_applied: List saved, but the server did not apply it. The reason is shown above the list.
blocklist.error_too_wide: Too wide: at most /8 for IPv4 and /16 for IPv6
blocklist.error_special: Not a public address: local, special and multicast addresses cannot be blocked
blocklist.error_invalid: Does not look like an address or network
blocklist.error_covers: Overlaps {{prefix}} from the list: keep one of them
blocklist.error_too_many: The list holds at most {{max}} entries
blocklist.status_leftover_one: The server still has {{count}} rule from an earlier install that the panel does not know. The panel removes it within a minute.
blocklist.status_leftover_other: The server still has {{count}} rules from an earlier install that the panel does not know. The panel removes them within a minute.
blocklist.status_leftover_waiting_one: The server still has {{count}} rule from an earlier install. The panel removes it once the server is connected.
blocklist.status_leftover_waiting_other: The server still has {{count}} rules from an earlier install. The panel removes them once the server is connected.
blocklist.conflict: Someone changed the list in another window a moment ago. The fresh list is loaded; make your change again.
